sentences.text: Effigia possessed a bipedal stance, a long neck, and a toothless beaked skull that closely resembled Cretaceous ornithomimid dinosaurs.
This two-meter-long animal was recovered from fossil blocks excavated at the Ghost Ranch quarry.
The species was named in January 2006 after Georgia O'Keeffe, whose ashes were scattered at the same Ghost Ranch site.
The full scientific name, Effigia okeeffeae, was formally established by Nesbitt and Mark Norell in January 2006.
The holotype fossil, which serves as the specimen the species is based on, was collected by Edwin H. Colbert in 1947.
Colbert had originally collected these fossil blocks intending to find Coelophysis and believed no other large vertebrates were present.
Biomechanical studies indicate Effigia could not peck for food like ostriches because its skull could not withstand such forces.
Effigia was a poposauroid pseudosuchian whose closest living relatives are crocodilians, not dinosaurs.
The animal belongs to the family Poposauridae.
It is classified within the order Rauisuchia.
Taxonomically, Effigia is placed within the unranked order Crurotarsi.
The resemblance of Effigia to ornithomimid dinosaurs is an example of extreme convergent evolution.
A 2007 proposal to synonymize Effigia with Shuvosaurus was not accepted by Nesbitt.
Effigia lived during the Late Triassic period.
Fossils are known from the Late Triassic of New Mexico in the southwestern USA.
The animal lived during the Upper Triassic.
Effigia lived from 205.7 to 201.4 million years ago during the Rhaetian stage.
